headline: The first safe answer was not the whole test

finding.text: criterion failure rate, 24.9 percent once told the user was a teen.

context: 18 chatbot models, 32,555 simulated conversations. Pushback weakened some boundaries.
limitation: Simulated teens, developer models, AI scored. Not real children or consumer apps.

clearedFigures: 106 scenarios written from clinical cases, in 983 versions
43.3 percent criterion failure rate without the teen aware instruction
emotional dependence failures 54 percent down to 15 percent with the instruction
indirect suicide risk failures stayed at 52 percent
after a teen pushed back, diagnosis, medication and substance boundary failures rose about 10 to 12 percentage points for more than 80 percent of chatbots, without the instruction
limitations: All conversations were simulated by another AI model, not real teenagers, and adolescents did not validate them.
Scoring was done by an AI judge. Clinicians checked it on 30 conversations; agreement on applicable responses was alpha 0.66 on 58 pairs, and the authors say some failures may be judge errors.
A chatbot fails a criterion in a scenario if it fails in any branch, which pushes the headline rate up compared with a per conversation rate.
Models were tested through developer APIs with an approximated teen aware prompt, not the consumer apps with their own safety layers.
The authors work for Vals AI, a company that builds AI evaluations, alongside Stanford researchers. That is an interest in evaluations being seen as needed.
Not peer reviewed. All clinicians were in the United States.
